title: Halloween
wiki_lead:
Halloween, also known as All Hallows' Eve or All Saints' Eve,  is a celebration observed in many countries  on 31 October, the eve of Western Christianity's feast of All Hallows' Day. It is at the beginning of the observance of Allhallowtide, the time in the Christian liturgical year dedicated to remembering the dead, including saints (hallows), Christian martyrs, and all the faithful departed. In popular culture, Halloween has become a celebration of horror and is associated with the macabre and the supernatural.
One theory holds that many Halloween traditions were influenced by Celtic harvest festivals, particularly the Gaelic festival Samhain, which is believed to have pagan roots. Some theories go further and suggest that Samhain may have been Christianized as All Hallows' Day, along with its eve, by the Christian Church. Other scholars say Halloween began independently as a Christian holiday, being the vigil of All Hallows' Day. Celebrated in Ireland and Scotland for centuries, Irish and Scottish immigrants brought many Halloween customs to North America in the 19th century. Through American influence, various Halloween customs spread to other countries by the late 20th and early 21st centuries.
Popular Halloween activities include trick-or-treating (or the related guising and souling), attending Halloween costume parties, carving pumpkins or turnips into jack-o'-lanterns, lighting bonfires, apple bobbing, divination games, playing pranks, visiting haunted attractions, telling frightening stories, and watching horror or Halloween-themed films. Some Christians practice the observances of All Hallows' Eve, including attending church services and lighting candles on the graves of the dead, although it is a secular celebration for others. Historically, some Christians abstained from meat on All Hallows' Eve, a tradition reflected in the eating of certain vegetarian foods on this day, including apples, potato pancakes, and soul cakes.

Some theories go further and suggest that Samhain may have been Christianized as All Hallows' Day, along with its eve, by the Christian Church. Other scholars say Halloween began independently as a Christian holiday, being the vigil of All Hallows' Day. Etymology

Hallow derives from Middle English halowen, from Old English hālig which means holy; it has been used synonymously with the word saint. The word Halloween or Hallowe'en comes from the Lowland Scots form of All Hallows' Eve (the evening before All Hallows' Day): even is the Scots term for 'eve' or 'evening', and is contracted to e'en or een; so (All) Hallow(s) E(v)en became Halloween. A term equivalent to 'All Hallows Eve' as attested in Old English. Thus, the name originates in Christianity, and means "Saints' eve(ning)".


History


Christian origins and historical customs

'Halloween' comes from All Hallows' Eve, being the night before All Hallows' Day (All Saints' Day), which is followed by All Souls' Day on 2 November. These three days are a part of Allhallowtide, a time when Western Christians honour all Christian martyrs and saints, as well as pray for departed souls. Halloween is influenced by Christian beliefs and practices surrounding these holy days. Christian holidays such as Christmas and Easter have vigils that begin the night before, as does All Hallows. 
After the persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire, "there were more martyrs than there were days in the year, and so one day was set apart in honor of them all, and called All Saints' Day." Commemorations of all saints and martyrs were held by several churches on various dates, mostly in springtime. In 4th-century Roman Edessa it was held on 13 May, and that date was endorsed by Pope Boniface IV in 609, when he re-dedicated the Pantheon in Rome to Mary and all martyrs. This was the date of Lemuria, an ancient Roman festival of the dead, when it was believed that restless and vengeful souls wandered. Some folklorists also suggest the ancient Roman festival of Parentalia (including Feralia) influenced All Saints' and All Souls' days. Parentalia involved a commemorative meal at the graves of relatives, during which food and drink were offered to the dead. Despite opposition from Church leaders, Christian Romans continued this custom, extending it to the saints and martyrs.
There is evidence that by 800, churches in Ireland and Northumbria were holding a feast commemorating all saints on 1 November. In 835, the Frankish Empire officially adopted 1 November as the date of All Saints' Day, which was endorsed by Pope Gregory IV. This may have been promoted by Alcuin of Northumbria, who was a member of Charlemagne's court, or by the Irish clerics and scholars who were also members of the Frankish court. The date was influenced by Celtic or Germanic idea traditions commemorating the dead at the beginning of winter. They may have seen it as the most fitting time to do so, as it is a time of "dying" in nature. It is also suggested the change was made on the "practical grounds that Rome in summer could not accommodate the great number of pilgrims who flocked to it", and perhaps because of public health concerns over Roman Fever, which claimed a number of lives during Rome's summers.

All Souls' Day, a feast commemorating all deceased Christians, became widespread in the 12th century. Its date was fixed on 2 November, the day after All Saints', and by the end of the century, both had become important holy days in Western Christianity. On All Souls' Day, people prayed for the dead and church bells were rung for souls in Purgatory. It was also customary for criers dressed in black to walk the streets "ringing a mournful bell and calling on all people to remember the poor souls in purgatory".
The All Souls' Day custom of baking and sharing soul cakes for all christened souls has been suggested as the origin of trick-or-treating. Called "souling", the custom dates back at least as far as the 15th century and was found in parts of England, Wales, Flanders, Southern Germany and Austria. Groups of poor people, often children, would go door to door on All Souls' Day, collecting soul cakes in exchange for praying for the dead, especially the souls of the givers' friends and relatives. Soul cakes were also offered for the souls themselves to eat, being laid on graves, or the "soulers" would act as their representatives. It has been suggested that this replaced the pre-Christian custom of offering food to the dead. As with the Lenten tradition of hot cross buns, soul cakes were often marked with a cross, indicating that they were baked as alms. In parts of the British Isles, "soulers" carried lanterns made of hollowed-out turnips, which might have originally represented souls in purgatory; later jack-o'-lanterns were used to ward off evil spirits.
Christian minister Prince Sorie Conteh linked the wearing of costumes to the belief in vengeful ghosts: "It was traditionally believed that the souls of the departed wandered the earth until All Saints' Day, and All Hallows' Eve provided one last chance for the dead to gain vengeance on their enemies before moving to the next world. In order to avoid being recognized by any soul that might be seeking such vengeance, people would don masks or costumes". According to Lesley Bannatyne, in the Middle Ages, churches in Europe that were too poor to display relics of martyred saints on All Hallows' Day let parishioners dress up as saints instead. Bannatyne opines that this "resembled the pagan custom of parading ghosts to the town limits". Some Christians observe this custom at Halloween today. Many Christians in mainland Europe believed "that once a year, on Hallowe'en, the dead of the churchyards rose for one wild, hideous carnival" known as the danse macabre; compositions have celebrated this belief. It has been suggested as an origin of Halloween costumes. Often depicted in church decoration, the danse macabre urged Christians "not to forget the end of all earthly things". According to an article in Christianity Today, the danse macabre was sometimes enacted in European village pageants and court masques with people "dressing up as corpses from various strata of society".
In Britain, a number of these customs came under attack during the Reformation, as Protestants berated Purgatory as a "popish" doctrine incompatible with the Reformed (Calvinist) doctrine of predestination held by the Anglican Church. State-sanctioned ceremonies associated with the intercession of saints and prayer for souls in Purgatory were abolished during the Elizabethan reform, though All Hallows' Day remained in the Anglican liturgical calendar to commemorate saints as outstanding Christians rather than "semi-divine intercessors". For Protestants, the theology of Allhallowtide was redefined: "souls cannot be journeying from Purgatory on their way to Heaven, as Catholics frequently believe and assert. Instead, the so-called ghosts are thought to be in actuality evil spirits". In parts of England, some Protestants, as well as Catholics, continued souling, candlelit processions, or ringing church bells for the dead; but the Anglican Church eventually suppressed this bell-ringing. Professor of medieval archaeology Mark Donnelly and historian Daniel Diehl write that "barns and homes were blessed to protect people and livestock from the effect of witches, who were believed to accompany the malignant spirits as they traveled the earth".

After 1605, Allhallowtide in England was eclipsed by Guy Fawkes Night (5 November), which appropriated some of its customs. There, the ending of official Hallowmas ceremonies led to the development of new, unofficial customs. In 18th- and 19th-century rural Lancashire, Catholic families gathered on hills on the night of All Hallows' Eve and one person held a bunch of burning straw on a pitchfork while the rest knelt around him, praying for the souls of relatives and friends until the flames went out. This was known as teen'lay. There was a similar custom in Hertfordshire, and the lighting of "tindle" fires in Derbyshire. Robert A. Davis suggests that bonfires during Allhallowtide referenced "God's instrument of purgation and penance", part of the theology of Christian repentance. Some suggested that candles, lit stoves and fires were originally lit to "guide the poor souls back to earth". Scottish Halloween customs survived the Calvinist Reformation and Guy Fawkes Night because the Presbyterian Church of Scotland acknowledged they were important to "the life cycle and rites of passage of local communities", and would be difficult to stamp out.
There is evidence that by the 16th century, in parts of Europe, it was customary to visit graves at Allhallowtide, "presenting offerings of flowers, candles, and food to deceased relatives". In southern Italy, it was customary during the Middle Ages to set food on the table for wandering souls before leaving for church services. This was banned in the 15th century as being a remnant of a pagan ritual, although the custom also drew thieves. By the 19th century, on All Souls' Eve, food was still left overnight for returning souls in the Abruzzi, Tyrol, the Vosges, Brittany, and Ireland. Candles were also lit in households in these regions, as well as in Ireland, Brittany, Flanders, Bavaria, Bohemia, and Tyrol, to "guide the souls back to visit their earthly homes". The Tyrolean "soul lights" were lamps filled with lard or butter. On All Souls' Day in 19th century Brittany, Catholics also poured libations of milk on the graves of kinfolk, while in Bavaria, Catholics laid soul cakes on graves to feed the hungry souls.
In the 19th century, some Italian churches staged "theatrical re-enactments of scenes from the lives of the saints" on All Hallows' Day, with "participants represented by realistic wax figures". In 1823, the graveyard of Holy Spirit Hospital in Rome presented a scene in which bodies of those who recently died were arrayed around a wax statue of an angel who pointed upward towards heaven. In the same country, "parish priests went house-to-house, asking for small gifts of food which they shared among themselves throughout that night". grok_lead: Halloween is an annual holiday celebrated on October 31, primarily in countries of the Western world such as the United States, Canada, Ireland, and the United Kingdom, featuring activities like costume-wearing, trick-or-treating, carving jack-o'-lanterns, and hosting parties with games and seasonal treats. The holiday's roots trace back over 2,000 years to the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain (pronounced "SAH-win"), observed by the Celts in what is now Ireland, the United Kingdom, and northern France to mark the end of the harvest season and the onset of winter, which was seen as a time when the boundary between the living world and the spirit realm thinned, allowing ghosts and fairies to roam freely. During Samhain, Celts lit bonfires to honor the harvest and ward off evil spirits, while later accounts describe participants wearing costumes or disguisesâoften animal skins or masksâto blend in with or frighten away wandering souls, though direct evidence for this as an ancient Celtic practice is limited. Communities also left food offerings outside homes for these spirits, a practice that foreshadowed later traditions like trick-or-treating. In the 8th century, Christian missionaries influenced the festival by designating November 1 as All Saints' Day (also known as All Hallows' Day) to honor saints and martyrs, shifting the focus from pagan rituals to Christian reverence while retaining many Samhain customs on the preceding evening, which became known as All Hallows' Eve or Halloween. This blending incorporated elements like the Roman festival of Pomona ( goddess of fruit and seeds), which contributed traditions such as bobbing for apples, symbolizing fertility and harvest. By the 9th century, the holiday had spread across Europe, with practices like "guising"âchildren dressing up and begging for treatsâemerging in Scotland and Ireland as early as the 16th century to commemorate the souls in purgatory. Halloween evolved further with Irish and Scottish immigrants bringing traditions to North America in the mid-19th century, where the pumpkin ânative to the Americasâreplaced turnips for carving jack-o'-lanterns, inspired by the Irish legend of Stingy Jack, a man doomed to wander with a lantern made from a carved vegetable. In the United States, the holiday gained popularity in the late 19th and early 20th centuries through community events and school activities, but trick-or-treating as a widespread custom surged in the 1940s and 1950s amid post-World War II suburban growth and increased candy production, transforming Halloween into a commercialized celebration of fun, fright, and fall festivities. Today, it emphasizes secular entertainment while echoing its ancient themes of harvest, the supernatural, and communal bonding.
